Crossover from Wannier-Stark localization to charge density waves for interacting spinless fermions in one dimension

August 24, 2026
Abstract

We study spinless fermions on a finite chain with nearest-neighbor repulsion and in the presence of a Wannier-Stark linearly-varying electric field potential. In the absence of the interaction, the eigenstates are localized for the system’s sizes larger than the localization length. We present several analytical expressions for the localization length, which is proportional to the inverse of the electric field. Using the density matrix renormalization group numerical technique, we observe that the ground state exhibits a decrease of the occupation on the chain sites from the ‘bulk’, with occupation 1, to the vacuum, with occupation 0. The width of this intermediate ‘edge’ region is also inversely proportional to the electric field, increasing linearly with the strength of the nearest-neighbor repulsion. For strong interactions, the occupations in the intermediate region exhibit a charge density wave. We also present the local density of states for sites in the ‘edge’ region. For the non-interacting case, the spectrum shows an increasing energy-localized structure as the field is increased, which is a consequence of the uniform energy distribution of the localized states (Wannier-Stark ladder). This structure survives for small interactions, and it smears out in the strongly interacting limit. Experimental variations of the slope of the potential (the electric field) on cold atom chains may test these predictions.

I Introduction

One-dimensional cold atom chains have been the center of much recent experimental and theoretical interest [1, 2]. In particular, such chains can be used to study the edge that separates the fully occupied insulating ‘bulk’ and the empty vacuum. Such an edge can be generated by a confining potential, which increases as one moves away from the bulk. Recently, we have studied such confinements caused by a linear potential, i.e., a constant electric field [3, 4]. It has been shown that the competition between linear potential and electron-electron interactions can produce a rich coexistence of locally ordered structures along the ‘edge’. Here we concentrate on the special case of spinless particles.

Even without interactions, the simultaneous effects of a periodic potential and a static electric field on electrons have been an important topic in condensed matter physics [6, 7, 8]. This research started many years ago when Wannier (among many others) argued that the application of an electric field FF turns the continuum of Bloch states induced by the periodic potential into an equally spaced ladder of discrete energy states, with the spacing given by e​a​FeaF [9]. Here −e-e (e>0e>0) is the electron charge, and aa is the lattice constant. This has been known as the Wannier-Stark (WS) ladder. The WS eigenstates are localized, leading to the corresponding Bloch oscillations [6, 7, 8, 10]. The Bloch oscillations are the counterparts in the time domain of the stationary states represented by the WS ladder in the energy domain. While for some time the existence of the WS ladder and Bloch oscillations was controversial, they are now firmly established; they have been observed in semiconductor devices [11, 12, 13, 14] and accelerated optical lattices [15, 16, 17, 18, 19].

Theoretically, the energy spectrum and eigenfunctions of non-interacting tightly bound electrons in a uniform electric field have been studied for finite and infinite chains [20]. In the latter case, both the WS energy spectrum and the associated eigenfunctions have been obtained analytically in terms of Bessel functions. In the present paper, we extend these analytical results for the non-interacting WS localization length, the site occupations of the fermions in the ground state of the many-particle states, and the localized density of states. We show that the analytical expressions for the infinite chain are fully recovered for sufficiently long finite chains. All the localization lengths turn out to be inversely proportional to FF.

While in the case analyzed in Ref. [20] all the eigenstates are more than exponentially localized, some recent papers claimed the existence of mobility edges in generalized WS lattices, termed “mosaic" WS lattices  [21, 22]. This is unexpected, as mobility edges separating localized from extended states are prevented in disorder-free low-dimensional systems [23]. However, the issue seems to have been settled, as it has been rigorously found that the energy spectrum is discrete even for these “mosaic" WS lattices, except a few isolated extended states [24].

The main features of WS physics have been recently extended from the electron to the phonon domain in Ref. [25]. The results suggested that the classical motion of a one-dimensional chain of atoms coupled through a specific force function that depends on position shows features very similar to the electronic WS counterpart, for instance localized phonon modes and phonon Bloch oscillations.

The main subject of this paper concerns the interacting Wannier-Stark fermionic lattice: electrons under the combination of a periodic potential, a constant electric field, and interactions. The underlying physics in these systems is sometimes referred to as the “Stark Many-Body Localization" (SMBL)  [26, 27, 28, 29]. The issue has received increasing recent attention due to its possible connection to the hot topic of Many-Body Localization (MBL), which concerns the interplay between disorder, localization, and interactions [30]. In the case of SMBL, the systems are disorder-free, but they seem to exhibit non-ergodic features and then constitute a class of generic nonrandom systems that fail to thermalize. Thus, the main physical feature that characterizes MBL, is that it is localization, and not disorder, that matters for attaining non-ergodic behavior. In the present case, the particle localization is provided by the electric field.

At this time, it is not clear how the MBL phenomena relate to the details of the static many-body wave function of the electrons. In particular, some of the above references find such non-ergodic phenomena only when they remove some degeneracy by adding non-linear terms to the confining potential. In the present paper, we do not dwell on the non-ergodic features but concentrate on the characterization of the many-body wave functions. In particular, we study how the localization length induced by the electric field changes with interactions. In preparation for this question, we present an extensive analysis of the WS localization length for the non-interacting case, by analytical and numerical means.

Specifically, we study a tight-binding model of interacting spinless particles, on a finite one-dimensional lattice of LL sites and open boundary conditions. Setting the confining linear electric potential to vanish at the center of the chain, the resulting particle-hole symmetry between the two sides of the chain yields an average half-filling for the whole system. Without interactions, the linear potential is known to have the WS localized eigenstates. For a tunneling amplitude tt between nearest-neighbor sites, dimensional analysis shows that the localization length (and any other length) characterizing these states must be proportional to t/(e​a​F)t/(eaF). Below we give explicit expressions for the pre-factors. The sites of the chain are fully occupied at the far left of the chain (large negative local potential), representing the ‘bulk’, and fully empty at the far right of the chain (large positive local potential), representing the vacuum. The intermediate region, in which the site occupation decreases from 1 to 0, forms a domain wall between the fully occupied ‘bulk’ and the completely empty vacuum. We refer to this ‘active’ region as the ’edge’. For the non-interacting case, we show that the width of this intermediate domain is directly related to the single-particle localization length, growing linearly with t/(e​F)t/(eF). We show that finite interactions broaden the intermediate region between the bulk and the vacuum, which still grows linearly with t/(e​F)t/(eF) with a pre-factor that depends on the tunneling and the interaction. For strong interactions, the repulsion between nearest-neighbor sites generates a charge density wave (CDW) within the domain wall. At half-filling, the occupations along the intermediate domain are ...101010​…...101010.... Similar effects due to nearest-neighbor interaction were found in earlier papers [3, 4, 5]. We study the crossover between the different regimes.

Except for the analytic expressions derived for the infinite chains, all our results for the finite chains are numerical, using the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method [31, 32]. This method allows us to find the ground state (GS) of the interacting many-body system for a finite one-dimensional lattice. In the non-interacting case, this GS is the Slater determinant of the single-particle WS-occupied states. We present results for different sizes of the system, all of which have occupation 1 on the left and 0 on the right so that we avoid finite size effects. Specifically, we used the matrix product state [33] implementation of the DMRG to perform the calculations, keeping around five hundred states and less than a dozen sweeps in each calculation.

Section II defines our model. Results for the non-interacting case are given in Sec. III, which compares analytical expressions with numerical estimates for the site occupations, different compatible definitions of the localization length, their relation to the size of the ‘domain walls’, and the local density of states. The results for the same quantities in the interacting case are given in Sec. IV, where the occupations in the center of the chain develop into a charge density wave. Section V contains our conclusions.

II The Model

We study interacting spinless fermions described by a tight-binding Hamiltonian on an open one-dimensional lattice of LL sites with lattice parameter aa,

H^=H^t+H^p​o​t+H^i​n​t.\displaystyle\hat{H}=\hat{H}_{t}+\hat{H}_{pot}+\hat{H}_{int}\ . (1)

The tunneling Hamiltonian is

H^t=\displaystyle\hat{H}_{t}= −t∑j(c^j+1†c^j+c^j†c^j+1).\displaystyle-t\sum_{j}\left(\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j+1}\hat{c}_{j}+\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{c}_{j+1}\right)\ . (2)

Here tt is the nearest-neighbor tunneling amplitude, and c^j†\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j} creates a fermion at site jj. These fermions are subjected to a linear potential,

H^p​o​t=\displaystyle\hat{H}_{pot}= ∑jμj​c^j†​c^j,\displaystyle\sum_{j}\mu_{j}\;\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{c}_{j}\ , (3)

where

μj=e​a​F​(j−jc),\displaystyle\mu_{j}=eaF\left(j-j_{c}\right)\ , (4)

is the site-dependent potential due to the external electric field. This potential is set to vanish at the center of the chain, jcj_{c}, to ensure particle-hole symmetry between the two halves of the system. In the case of even (odd) LL, the potential vanishes at the central link (site), and jc=1/2j_{c}=1/2 (jc=0j_{c}=0). Our results are presented for an even LL. The fermions interact via the repulsive nearest-neighbor interaction, VV,

H^i​n​t=V​∑j(n^j−1/2)​(n^j+1−1/2),\displaystyle\hat{H}_{int}=V\sum_{j}(\hat{n}_{j}-1/2)(\hat{n}_{j+1}-1/2), (5)

where n^j=c^j†​c^j\hat{n}_{j}=\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{c}_{j} is the occupation operator. A sketch of the system is portrayed in Fig. 1.

III The non-interacting case: Analytical Results

III.1 The Bessel transformation

Except for a constant shift in the linear potential, the Hamiltonian in the absence of the repulsion reads

H^0=−t∑j(c^j+1†c^j+c^j†c^j+1)+eaF∑jjc^j†c^j,\displaystyle\hat{H}_{0}=-t\sum_{j}\left(\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j+1}\hat{c}_{j}+\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{c}_{j+1}\right)+eaF\sum_{j}j\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{c}_{j}\ , (6)

For the infinite chain, the well-known [20] eigenvalues of H^0\hat{H}_{0} are Em=e​a​F​mE_{m}=eaFm, with an integer mm, and eigenfunctions |m⟩=b^m†​|v​a​c⟩|m\rangle=\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{m}|{vac}\rangle, where |v​a​c⟩|{vac}\rangle is the vacuum, and

b^m†=∑j=−∞∞𝒥j−m​[2​t/(e​a​F)]​c^j†.\displaystyle\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{m}=\sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty}\mathscr{J}_{j-m}[2t/(eaF)]\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}\ . (7)

Here, 𝒥j−m​(x)\mathscr{J}_{j-m}(x) is the cylindrical Bessel function of the first kind of order j−mj-m. Thus, H^0\hat{H}_{0} is diagonalized,

H^0=e​a​F​∑mm​b^m†​b^m.\displaystyle\hat{H}_{0}=eaF\sum_{m}m\;\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{m}\hat{b}_{m}\ . (8)

In the limit of large FF, 𝒥j−m​[2​t/(e​a​F)]→δj,m\mathscr{J}_{j-m}[2t/(eaF)]\rightarrow\delta_{j,m}, and b^m†→c^j†\displaystyle\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{m}\rightarrow\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}, with m=jm=j. Note that while mm is an energy-related index, jj is a site-related index. Interestingly, both become intermixed in the building of the non-interacting eigenstates in Eq. (7), and finally they merge to become the same index for strong electric fields.

In the following, the tunneling amplitude tt is set to be the energy scale, and in most of the equations, e=a=ℏ=1e=a=\hbar=1, except where they are needed for clarity.

An important message embodied behind the excellent agreement seen in Fig. 2 is that, for sufficiently large LL, no finite-size effects appear in the numerical calculations, which are necessarily performed on finite chains (L=48L=48 in Fig. 2). This is because the intermediate region with non-integer filling is totally contained inside the finite system, while the inert regions with filling 1 and 0 at the extremes of the chain can be replaced by an infinite chain with no consequence on the physics in the bulk. For that reason, we also obtain an excellent fit when we truncate the sum in Eq. (11) to m≥−L/2+1m\geq-L/2+1; the omitted terms are too small to matter.

III.3 Charge distribution in the continuum limit

Using an integral representation [35] for the squares of the Bessel functions, an exact formula can be derived for njn_{j} when the subscript jj in Eq. (11) becomes continuous,

nj​(2F)=12−\displaystyle n_{j}\left(\frac{2}{F}\right)=\frac{1}{2}-
−12​π∫0π𝒥0[4Fsin(θ2)]sin⁡[(j−1/2)​θ]sin⁡(θ/2)dθ.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\mathscr{J}_{0}\left[\frac{4}{F}\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]~\frac{\sin\left[\left(j-1/2\right)\theta\right]}{\sin\left(\theta/2\right)}\;d\theta\ . (17)

Details of the derivation are given in Appendix A. Note that n1/2​(2/F)=1/2n_{1/2}(2/F)=1/2, independent of the strength of the electric field. For 4/F→04/F\rightarrow 0, the zero-order Bessel function in the integrand of Eq. (17) approaches 1, and n0​(2/F→0)→1n_{0}(2/F\rightarrow 0)\rightarrow 1, while n1​(2/F→0)→0n_{1}(2/F\rightarrow 0)\rightarrow 0. These limits imply a finite length of the intermediate region.

Figure 3 compares numerical results with those derived from Eq. (17), for F=0.2F=0.2, F=2F=2 and F→∞F\to\infty. The numerical numbers practically coincide with those derived from Eq. (11). As seen, Eq. (17) produces an oscillatory behavior that increases with FF. These oscillations are not reflected in the occupations for integer jj’s.

III.4 Localization lengths

In all panels in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 there appear three regions: on the left - the occupied ‘bulk’ segment, with nj=1n_{j}=1, on the right - the empty ‘vacuum’, with nj=0n_{j}=0, and the intermediate zone in which njn_{j} decreases monotonically from 11 to 00. Here, we estimate the width of this intermediate region, which may be considered as a domain wall in the occupation number profile. Dimensional analysis shows that this width must be proportional to t/(e​F)t/(eF). We present several possible definitions for it and show that they are indeed all proportional to t/Ft/F, i.e., inversely proportional to the electric field.

III.4.1 Estimation based on the bandwidth

One way to estimate the width of the intermediate-filling region follows by adapting the argument of Ref. [4]: For the non-interacting fermions, a certain site jj is occupied when μj≲− 2​t\mu_{j}\lesssim-\;2t band edge of the non-interacting system) and is empty for μj≳2​t\mu_{j}\gtrsim 2t. Exploiting Eq. (4), the two cases can be presented as

μ<\displaystyle\mu_{<} =e​a​F​(j<−jc)=−2​t,\displaystyle=eaF(j_{<}-j_{c})=-2t\ ,
μ>\displaystyle\mu_{>} =e​a​F​(j>−jc)=+2​t,\displaystyle=eaF(j_{>}-j_{c})=+2t\ , (18)

leading to an intermediate region of length

j>−j<=4​te​a​F,\displaystyle j_{>}-j_{<}=\frac{4t}{eaF}\ , (19)

(4/F4/F in our dimensionless unit scheme). This estimate has been previously derived in Ref. [20], based on numerical analysis. As the derivation suggests, Eq. (19) works well when the size of the domain wall involves several sites of the chain; however, it approaches zero in the strong electric field limit. As the domain wall cannot be narrower than the lattice parameter (1 in our dimensionless units), we propose to define the localization length as

ξ1=4F+1.\displaystyle\xi_{1}=\frac{4}{F}+1\ . (20)

ξ1\xi_{1} is displayed by the orange full line in Fig. 4.

From Eq. (11) for the single-particle filling it follows that the region with intermediate filling begins at the site where there is a finite probability of finding a hole [1-𝒥m−j2​(x)\mathscr{J}^{2}_{m-j}(x)] and ends at the site with zero probability of finding an electron [𝒥m−j2​(x)\mathscr{J}^{2}_{m-j}(x)]. The distance between these two points determines the width of the single-particle wave function for a given quantum number mm. Hence, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the width of the single-particle wave function and the width of the intermediate region ξ1\xi_{1}.

III.4.2 Estimation based on the intermediate-filling region

An alternative estimation of the intermediate-filling region width is obtained by taking into account all sites with occupation ε<nj<1−ε\varepsilon<n_{j}<1-\varepsilon, where ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1. Whether we use Eq. (17) for the occupation njn_{j} at continuous jj or the njn_{j} obtained by the DMRG, we can define jR>0j_{R}>0 as the largest site jj whose filling obeys

njR≥ε.\displaystyle n_{j_{R}}\geq\varepsilon\ . (21)

The corresponding size of the domain wall is then

ξ2=2​jR,\displaystyle\xi_{2}=2\;j_{R}\;, (22)

with the factor of 2 accounting for the chain sites with negative jj. The results of Eq. (22) using Eq. (17) for the occupation are displayed by open circles in Fig. 4. As seen, ξ2\xi_{2} approaches 11 in the strong-field limit without any adjustment, as expected. Also, note that the characteristic length 4/F4/F appears quite naturally in the argument of the Bessel function of order zero in Eq. (17), controlling the range where the occupation function njn_{j} deviates from 1 at the left and from 0 at the right (Fig. 3).

III.4.3 Single-particle localization length

A natural definition of the localization length of a single-particle wave function is given by its average width, for example, for a particle with the quantum number m=0m=0 (the definition being independent of this quantum number),

ξ~=∑j=−∞∞j2​pj​(0),\displaystyle\tilde{\xi}=\sqrt{\sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty}j^{2}p_{j}(0)}\ , (23)

where pj​(0)=𝒥j2​(2/F)p_{j}(0)=\mathscr{J}_{j}^{2}(2/F) is the probability of finding the single electron at site jj when it has been created in the Wannier-Stark eigenstate |m=0⟩=b^0†|vac⟩|m=0\rangle=\hat{b}_{0}^{\dagger}|vac\rangle [see Eq. (11)]. This is a particular case of the more general expression,

pj​(m)=|⟨v​a​c|c^j​b^m†|v​a​c⟩|2=𝒥j−m2​(2/F),\displaystyle p_{j}(m)=|\langle{vac}|\hat{c}_{j}\hat{b}_{m}^{\dagger}|{vac}\rangle|^{2}=\mathscr{J}_{j-m}^{2}(2/F)\;, (24)

which is the probability of finding the single electron at site jj, when created in the eigenstate |m⟩=b^m†​|v​a​c⟩|m\rangle=\hat{b}_{m}^{\dagger}|vac\rangle. Using the Bessel functions’ identity [34]

𝒥j−1​(x)+𝒥j+1​(x)=(2​j/x)​𝒥j​(x)\mathscr{J}_{j-1}(x)+\mathscr{J}_{j+1}(x)=(2j/x)\mathscr{J}_{j}(x) (25)

and Eq. (12) derived for the infinite chain, we obtain

ξ~2​(x)=∑j=−∞∞|j​𝒥j​(x)|2=2​(x/2)2=2​(t/F)2.\displaystyle\tilde{\xi}^{2}(x)=\sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty}|j\mathscr{J}_{j}(x)|^{2}=2(x/2)^{2}=2(t/F)^{2}\ . (26)

ξ~\tilde{\xi} is inversely propotional to the electric field, t/Ft/F, as expected from dimensional analysis. Interestingly enough, defining

ξ3​(x)=2​2​ξ~​(x)+1,\displaystyle\xi_{3}(x)=2\sqrt{2}\;\tilde{\xi}(x)+1\;, (27)

the single-particle localization length as defined in Eq. (26) becomes identical to ξ1​(x)\xi_{1}(x), Eq. (20). Our results show that ξ3\xi_{3}, which represents the well-documented exponential localization of the Wannier-Stark eigenstates, together with ξ1\xi_{1} and ξ2\xi_{2}, which represent the width of the domain wall of the occupation number function, are just different ways of quantifying the same Wannier-Stark localization physics. See, however, Ref. [36].

III.4.4 Many-particle localization length

We define the many-particle localization length as the mean-square distance of the charge distribution:

ξ~~=2​∑j>0(j−jc)2​p~j,\displaystyle\tilde{\tilde{\xi}}=2\sqrt{\sum_{j>0}(j-j_{c})^{2}\tilde{p}_{j}}\ , (28)

where pj​(0)p_{j}(0) in Eq. (23) is replaced by p~j≡nj/𝒩\tilde{p}_{j}\equiv n_{j}/{\cal N}, with 𝒩=∑j′>0nj′{\cal N}=\sum_{j^{\prime}>0}n_{j^{\prime}} being the total probability of finding electrons on the right-hand side of the chain (equal to the total number of holes on the left-hand side). Note that jc=1/2j_{c}=1/2 for even LL. The sum runs only on j>0j>0, where njn_{j} decreases from 1/21/2 to zero, the factor of 2 accounting for the negative jj’s. We shall use the same definition when including the interaction between the fermions in the discussion.

The analytic expression for ξ~~\tilde{\tilde{\xi}} for non-interacting fermions is worked out in Appendix B. It is compared with the DMRG results for the ground state of non-interacting fermions (V=0V=0) in Fig. 4, utilizing for convenience the expression

ξ4=A4​ξ~~+B4,\displaystyle\xi_{4}=A_{4}\tilde{\tilde{\xi}}+B_{4}\;, (29)

where the constants A4=2.13A_{4}=2.13 and B4=0.88B_{4}=0.88 are adjusted for fitting it with Eq. (20). The matching of the field-dependence of ξ4\xi_{4} with the other lengths justifies using Eq. (29) also for estimating the localization length of interacting fermions, carried out in Sec. IV.

III.5 The local density of states for non-interacting fermions

The local density of states (LDOS) is calculated by applying Zubarev’s equation-of-motion method [7] to the Hamiltonian H^0\hat{H}_{0}, Eq. (6). The frequency-dependent diagonal Green’s function gives the site-dependent density of states

Gj0​(ω)=−1π​Im​⟨⟨c^j;c^j†⟩⟩.\displaystyle G^{0}_{j}(\omega)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\;{\rm Im}\langle\langle\hat{c}_{j};\hat{c}_{j}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle\;. (30)

This Green’s function obeys the Dyson equation [7]

ω⁡⟨⟨c^j;c^j′†⟩⟩\displaystyle\omega\;\langle\langle\hat{c}_{j};\hat{c}_{j^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle =[c^j,c^j′†]++⟨⟨[c^j,H^0]±;c^j′†⟩⟩\displaystyle=[\hat{c}_{j},\hat{c}_{j^{\prime}}^{\dagger}]_{+}+\langle\langle[\hat{c}_{j},\hat{H}_{0}]_{\pm};\hat{c}_{j^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle
=δj,j′+⟨⟨[c^j,H^0]±;c^j′†⟩⟩.\displaystyle=\delta_{j,j^{\prime}}+\langle\langle[\hat{c}_{j},\hat{H}_{0}]_{\pm};\hat{c}_{j^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle\;. (31)

Here, [A^;B^]±[\hat{A};\hat{B}]_{\pm} denotes either the anti-conmutator (++) or commutator (−-) between operators A^\hat{A} and B^\hat{B}. Using the diagonal form of H^0\hat{H}_{0}, Eq. (8), the Dyson equation Eq. (31) becomes

ω⁡⟨⟨c^j;c^j′†⟩⟩\displaystyle\omega\;\langle\langle\hat{c}_{j};\hat{c}_{j^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle =δj,j′+F​∑m=−∞∞m​𝒥j−m​(2/F)\displaystyle=\delta_{j,j^{\prime}}+F\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}m\mathscr{J}_{j-m}(2/F)
×∑j′′=−∞∞𝒥j′′−m​(2/F)​⟨⟨c^j′′;c^j′†⟩⟩,\displaystyle\times\sum_{j^{\prime\prime}=-\infty}^{\infty}\mathscr{J}_{j^{\prime\prime}-m}(2/F)\langle\langle\hat{c}_{j^{\prime\prime}};\hat{c}_{j^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle\;, (32)

Multiplying both sides of Eq. (32) by 𝒥j′−m​(2/F)\mathscr{J}_{j^{\prime}-m}(2/F) and summing over j′j^{\prime} yields:

∑j′=−∞∞𝒥j′−m​(2/F)​⟨⟨c^j′;c^j†⟩⟩=𝒥j−m​(2/F)(ω−m​F).\displaystyle\sum_{j^{\prime}=-\infty}^{\infty}\mathscr{J}_{j^{\prime}-m}(2/F)\langle\langle\hat{c}_{j^{\prime}};\hat{c}_{j}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle=\frac{\mathscr{J}_{j-m}(2/F)}{(\omega-mF)}\;. (33)

Hence, for j=j′j=j^{\prime} and using Eq. (33) , Eq. (32) yields

⟨⟨c^j;c^j†⟩⟩=∑m=−∞∞𝒥j−m 2​(2/F)(ω−m​F).\displaystyle\langle\langle\hat{c}_{j};\hat{c}_{j}^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathscr{J}_{j-m}^{\;2}(2/F)}{(\omega-mF)}\;. (34)

Replacing ω→ω+i​η\omega\rightarrow\omega+i\eta with η→0\eta\to 0, that broadens the delta-function spikes, Eq. (30) becomes

Gj0​(ω)=ηπ​∑m𝒥j−m 2​(2/F)[ω−(m−jc)​F]2+η2,\displaystyle G^{0}_{j}(\omega)=\frac{\eta}{\pi}\sum_{m}\frac{\mathscr{J}^{\;2}_{j-m}(2/F)}{[\omega-(m-j_{c})F]^{2}+\eta^{2}}\;, (35)

which coincides with the result in Ref. [37] for η→0\eta\rightarrow 0. For small η\eta, this is a sum of Lorentzian functions centered at the different energy levels (m−jc)​F(m-j_{c})F weighted by the square of the corresponding Bessel function (‘the oscillator strength’). Calculating numerically the LDOS using the correction vector method [38] to obtain the Green’s function Gj​(ω)G_{j}(\omega) (details in Ref. [39]), results in an excellent agreement with Eq. (35), as depicted in Fig. 5. As the electric field FF increases, the oscillator strength becomes concentrated on a smaller number of peaks reflecting, in the frequency domain, the associated decreasing localization in real space of the Wannier-Stark eigenstates. For large electric fields, 𝒥j−m 2​(2/F)→δj,m\mathscr{J}^{\;2}_{j-m}(2/F)\rightarrow\delta_{j,m} and the LDOS becomes a single-peaked (Lorentzian-like) structure, centered at frequency ω=(j−jc)​F\omega=(j-j_{c})F. The localization length is proportional to the width of the region in real space whose site energy is contained within the energy support Δ​ω\Delta\omega of the LDOS ∼Δ​ω/F\sim\Delta\omega/F.

Finally, we mention that

nj=∫−∞0Gj0​(ω)​𝑑ω,\displaystyle n_{j}=\int_{-\infty}^{0}G^{0}_{j}(\omega)\;d\omega\;, (36)

is equal to the expression of the occupation number function given in Eq. (11).

IV Interacting Fermions

Currently, no analytical results are available for the Hamiltonian (1), which includes the interaction VV between the fermions. We thus resort to numerical calculations based on the DMRG.

IV.1 Charge distribution: Crossover to a charge density wave (CDW) region

The Wannier-Stark localized states characterizing the Hamiltonian in the absence of the interaction (V=0V=0) progressively turn into a charge density wave, with occupations alternating between 1 and 0, so that nj​nj+1=0n_{j}n_{j+1}=0, i.e., ...10101010​…...10101010... when VV is very strong. As might be expected, the competition between the interaction VV and the electric field FF is mainly significant around the center of the chain, where the site energy is not too negative (at the left) or too positive (at the right). We examine this competition in Figs. 6, 7, and 8. Note that in all these plots the particle-hole symmetry relation, n−j=1−nj+1n_{-j}=1-n_{j+1}, is obeyed.

Figure 6 presents the local (charge) occupations for a weak electric field FF and weak interactions, V≤2V\leq 2. As seen, there appear small oscillations in njn_{j} around the center of the chain as VV increases.

In the absence of an electric field, i.e., for a uniform chain, a charge density wave appears at a critical value, V=2V=2, of the interaction [40]. In the present case, the onset of the charge density wave appearing at larger values of the interaction is depicted in Figs. 7 and 8, both portraying a new region of charge density wave, whose width increases with VV. As mentioned, three different regions can be identified in the ground state: a band-insulating phase at the left and right regions (completely full and empty sites, respectively) and an ‘edge’ with strong CDW characteristics in the middle of the chain in between. This new region is separated from the band-insulating phases by ‘domain walls’ with non-integer fillings. As VV increases, it approaches the ‘pure’ CDW structure where nj​nj+1=0n_{j}n_{j+1}=0 (see Fig. 7). In contrast, increasing the electric field FF narrows down the central CDW domain while maintaining its intensity, as depicted in Fig. 8. This behavior provides the possibility of experimentally manipulating and controlling CDW-ordered regions within a confined system.

Contrary to the results obtained in the extended Hubbard model [4], we do not observe other CDW’s with different mean densities at other regions of the chain. This is a consequence of the fact that, for the uniform spinless model with nearest-neighbor interactions considered here, the only possible CDW is the one with the mean filling of 0.5 [40]. Instead, for the extended Hubbard model, there are CDW’s with different periodicities at mean fillings away from 1/2, e.g., 1/4.

We have calculated the size of the CDW region, LCDWL_{\text{CDW}}, and found that it has a linear dependence on 1/F1/F, as shown in Fig. 9. This size is obtained by calculating the charge-charge correlator ⟨nj​nj+1⟩\braket{n_{j}n_{j+1}} (top left inset in Fig. 9), when the order sets in this correlator is nearly constant and goes to zero for large VV. The boundaries of this region are obtained by setting a bound ϵ=0.001\epsilon=0.001 to the difference between the charge correlator and its mean value in the CDW region.

IV.2 Characteristic lengths

IV.2.1 Derivation based on the bandwidth of the Hamiltonian with interactions

Dimensional analysis implies that any typical length should be a linear combination of t/e​a​Ft/eaF and V/e​a​FV/eaF. Indeed, Wei et al. [29] use arguments similar to ours in Sec. III.4.1 to obtain an estimation of the width of this central region. For V≠0V\neq 0, the ‘band boundaries’ can be estimated by considering the energy of having only one particle in the system with respect to the empty system, −2​t−V-2t-V, for the lower limit, and the energy of having a completely filled band with respect to having one hole in the system, 2​t+V2t+V for the upper limit. Then, in the same spirit of Sec. III.4.1, we will have an intermediate occupation when −2​t−V<μj<2​t+V-2t-V<\mu_{j}<2t+V and the interacting version of Eq. (20) becomes:

ξ1,i​n​t=2​(2​t+V)/(e​F)+c,\displaystyle\xi_{1,int}=2\left(2t+V\right)/(eF)+c\ , (37)

where cc is a constant.

IV.2.2 Comparison with the intermediate-filling region ξ2\xi_{2} [Eq. (22)]

Figure 10 exhibits the results of the width of the interacting intermediate region where the numerically calculated density is 0<nj<10<n_{j}<1 and compares it with the analytical estimation described above. The scaled results for several values of the electric field FF and the interaction VV are in excellent agreement. This agreement induces us to define a localization length also for the many-body wave function. We find two scenarios for this model: one for small interactions, where no order arises in the intermediate region, and one for larger interactions, where a CDW is formed in this region, surrounded by two domain walls to the completely empty and full regions of the chain. In both cases, we can define a ‘localization’ length that is compatible with the one defined in the non-interacting case. This is possible because – for strong repulsion – the fermions are localized in the vicinity of the full and empty regions.

IV.2.3 Comparison with the many-particle localization length ξ4\xi_{4} [Eq. (29)] for small VV.

For V≤2​tV\leq 2t the site occupations in Fig. 6 are still qualitatively similar to those in the non-interacting case, except for the existence of density fluctuations within the intermediate region. As for this parameter range, there is no CDW, its width can be estimated using Eq. (29) numerically. Figure 11 portrays ξ4\xi_{4} versus 1/F1/F for L=150L=150 and for relatively small interactions, V=0V=0, 0.25, 0.5, and 1, showing a linear behavior. Again we find an excellent agreement with ξ1,i​n​t\xi_{1,int} as seen in the scaled inset.

IV.2.4 Local densities of state

The effect of a weak interaction on the localization length can also be observed in the structure of the local density of states. Figure 12 presents the evolution of the LDOS for F=2F=2, L=24L=24, and several values of VV obtained using DMRG. For the non-interacting case, as detailed before (Fig. 5), the LDOS has a well-defined discrete peak structure for this large value of FF, where the peaks are separated by the WS level splitting FF. Similar features have been observed in Ref. [41]. For small VV, this finite peak structure is modified and the total width is slightly increased, thus implying a larger localization length.

V Conclusions

We studied the ground state (GS) properties and local density of states (LDOS) of a spinless fermionic chain with nearest-neighbor repulsion VV in a linear Wannier-Stark (WS) potential. The competition between the (tunneling) kinetic energy, the repulsion, and the WS potential leads to the formation of regions with different characteristics. At the extreme left of the chain, there is a fully occupied zone, while at the extreme right, the sites are empty. On the left side, the site energies are very negative, so the sites are occupied irrespective of VV. Similarly, on the right-hand side the site energies are high, preventing their occupation.

In the middle region, there exists competition, leading to intermediate fillings with localized fermions. For V=0V=0 we present analytical results for the GS and LDOS, which match the numerical results using the DMRG when the localization length is smaller than the system size (and no finite-size dependence is found). This agreement serves as a test for the accuracy of our numerical DMRG (approximate) calculations. For finite values of VV, the intermediate region grows with VV. When V≤2​tV\leq 2t this region presents small filling fluctuations, while for V>2​tV>2t, a charge-density wave (CDW) is formed. This happens since around the middle of the chain, the chain is close to be half-filled because the site-varying potential lies within the charge gap. In this region, a CDW order is energetically preferable when VV is large enough (the critical value being Vc=2​tV_{c}=2t for the uniform case). It is worth noting that we do not find CDWs at other average fillings. Such fillings were found in similar studies for the extended Hubbard model [3, 4]. This is because for the Hamiltonian studied here, a CDW forms only at half-filling for the uniform case. The size of the CDW region increases with VV and decreases with FF, providing the possibility of experimentally manipulating and controlling CDW-ordered regions within a confined system.

The width of the intermediate region, between the fully occupied and the fully empty regions, is proportional to t/Ft/F. This is true in all the cases studied, including the localization length in the non-interacting WS ladder. In that case, the width is excellently approximated by its analytic value for the WS localization length in infinite chains. We presented several novel ways to measure this width. For the interacting case, this width is linear both in VV, and in 1/F1/F. The behavior of the LDOS also reflects the localization features observed from the static properties. Experimental variations of the slope of the potential (the electric field) on cold atom chains may be able of test these predictions.

Appendix A Derivation of Eq. (17) for the site occupation of a continuous jj

Our starting point is the integral representation of 𝒥n2​(x)\mathscr{J}^{2}_{n}(x) [35],

𝒥m−j2​(x)=12​π​∫−ππ𝒥0​(x,θ)​ei⁡(m−j)​θ​𝑑θ,𝒥0​(x,θ)=𝒥0​[2​x​sin⁡(θ/2)].\displaystyle\mathscr{J}^{2}_{m-j}(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\mathscr{J}_{0}(x,\theta)\;e^{i(m-j)\theta}d\theta\ ,\ \ \ \mathscr{J}_{0}(x,\theta)=\mathscr{J}_{0}[2x\sin(\theta/2)]\ . (38)

It follows that

∑m=1N𝒥m−j2​(x)\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{N}\mathscr{J}^{2}_{m-j}(x) =12​π​∫−ππ𝒥0​(x,θ)​∑m=1Nei​m​θ​e−i​j​θ​𝑑θ=12​π​∫−ππ𝒥0​(x,θ)​ei⁡(N+1/2)​θ−ei​θ/22​i​sin⁡(θ/2)​e−i​j​θ​𝑑θ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\mathscr{J}_{0}(x,\theta)\sum_{m=1}^{N}e^{im\theta}e^{-ij\theta}d\theta=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\mathscr{J}_{0}(x,\theta)\frac{e^{i(N+1/2)\theta}-e^{i\theta/2}}{2i\sin(\theta/2)}e^{-ij\theta}d\theta
=12​π​∫0π𝒥0​(x,θ)​{sin⁡[(j−1/2)​θ]sin⁡(θ/2)+sin⁡[(N+1/2−j)​θ]sin⁡(θ/2)}​𝑑θ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\mathscr{J}_{0}(x,\theta)\left\{\frac{\sin[(j-1/2)\theta]}{\sin(\theta/2)}+\frac{\sin[(N+1/2-j)\theta]}{\sin(\theta/2)}\right\}d\theta\ . (39)

Since the site occupation is given by

nj​(x)=∑m=−N0𝒥m−j2​(x)=1−∑m=1N𝒥m−j2​(x),\displaystyle n_{j}(x)=\sum_{m=-N}^{0}\mathscr{J}^{2}_{m-j}(x)=1-\sum_{m=1}^{N}\mathscr{J}^{2}_{m-j}(x)\ , (40)

we find

nj​(x)=1−12​π​∫0π𝒥0​(x,θ)​{sin⁡[(j−1/2)​θ]sin⁡(θ/2)+sin⁡[(N+1/2−j)​θ]sin⁡(θ/2)}​𝑑θ.\displaystyle n_{j}(x)=1-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\mathscr{J}_{0}(x,\theta)\left\{\frac{\sin[(j-1/2)\theta]}{\sin(\theta/2)}+\frac{\sin[(N+1/2-j)\theta]}{\sin(\theta/2)}\right\}d\theta\ . (41)

As shown in Ref. [35], the second term in the curly brackets vanishes in the N→∞N\rightarrow\infty limit, leading to Eq. (17) in the main text. Figure 2 indeed confirms that for integer jj’s, nj​(x)n_{j}(x) as given by Eq. (11) coincides with the one obtained from Eq. (17). Thus, for noninteger values of jj, Eq. (17) provides an interpolation scheme for the site occupations.

Interesting limits of Eq.(17), based on the derivation in Ref. [35], are: a) nj=1/2​(x)=1/2n_{j=1/2}(x)=1/2. The non-interacting occupation function nj​(x)n_{j}(x) is symmetric around the central point of the chain; b) nj→∞→0n_{j\rightarrow\infty}\rightarrow 0; and c) nj→−∞→1n_{j\rightarrow-\infty}\rightarrow 1.

ξ~~2\displaystyle\tilde{\tilde{\xi}}^{2} =116​x2+3128​x4−54608​x6+7147456​x8−1655360​x10+⋯,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{16}x^{2}+\frac{3}{128}x^{4}-\frac{5}{4608}x^{6}+\frac{7}{147456}x^{8}-\frac{1}{655360}x^{10}+\cdots\ ,
𝒩\displaystyle{\cal N} =14​x2−132​x4+1324​x6−536864​x8+71474560​x10+⋯.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}x^{2}-\frac{1}{32}x^{4}+\frac{1}{324}x^{6}-\frac{5}{36864}x^{8}+\frac{7}{1474560}x^{10}+\cdots. (49)

This does not give a linear ξA\xi_{A}, but as seen from the figure, the full expression is quite close to a straight line.

Appendix C Strong electric field limit

The Hamiltonian Eq. (1) can be expressed in terms of the operators {b^m,b^m†}\{\hat{b}_{m},\hat{b}_{m}^{\dagger}\} that diagonalize the Hamiltonian prevailing in the absence of the interaction, Eq. (6). Using the transformation {c^j,c^j†}=∑m𝒥j−m​(x)​{b^m,b^m†}\{\hat{c}_{j},\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{j}\}=\sum_{m}\mathscr{J}_{j-m}(x)\{\hat{b}_{m},\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{m}\} with x=2/Fx=2/F, one obtains

H^=F​∑mm​b^m†​b^m+V​∑m1,m2,m3,m4f⁡(m1,m2,m3,m4)​b^m1†​b^m2​b^1+m3†​b^1+m4,\displaystyle\hat{H}=F\sum_{m}m\;\hat{b}_{m}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{m}+V\sum_{m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},m_{4}}f(m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},m_{4})\;\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{m_{1}}\hat{b}_{m_{2}}\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{1+m_{3}}\hat{b}_{1+m_{4}}\ , (50)

where

f⁡(m1,m2,m3,m4)=∑j𝒥j−m1​(x)​𝒥j−m2​(x)​𝒥j−m3​(x)​𝒥j−m4​(x).\displaystyle f(m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},m_{4})=\sum_{j}\mathscr{J}_{j-m_{1}}(x)\mathscr{J}_{j-m_{2}}(x)\mathscr{J}_{j-m_{3}}(x)\mathscr{J}_{j-m_{4}}(x)\;. (51)

This Hamiltonian is simplified in the strong-field limit, i.e., for x→0x\rightarrow 0. Then, exploiting the series expansion of the Bessel functions for small arguments

𝒥ν​(z→0)→(z2)ν​[1+(−z2/4)Γ⁡(ν+2)+…],\displaystyle\mathscr{J}_{\nu}(z\rightarrow 0)\rightarrow\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{\nu}\left[1+\frac{(-z^{2}/4)}{\Gamma(\nu+2)}+...\right]\ , (52)

the leading contribution in the strong-field limit comes from the choice m1=m2=m3=m4=jm_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=j, where 𝒥0​(z→0)→1−z2/4+…\mathscr{J}_{0}(z\rightarrow 0)\rightarrow 1-z^{2}/4+.... The correction to the leading contribution comes from the choice j−m1=±1,m2=m3=m4=jj-m_{1}=\pm 1,m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=j, and the three equivalent choices obtained by exchanging the indexes m1,m2,m3,m4m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},m_{4}. In summary, in the strong-field limit, it is permissible to expand the range function f⁡(m1,m2,m3,m4)f(m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},m_{4}) as follows,

f⁡(m1,m2,m3,m4)\displaystyle f(m_{1},m_{2},m_{3},m_{4}) ≈δj,m1​δj,m2​δj,m3​δj,m4\displaystyle\approx\delta_{j,m_{1}}\delta_{j,m_{2}}\delta_{j,m_{3}}\delta_{j,m_{4}}
+x2(δj,m1±1δj,m2δj,m3δj,m4+m1↔m2+m1↔m3+m1↔m4)\displaystyle+\frac{x}{2}\big(\delta_{j,m_{1}\pm 1}\delta_{j,m_{2}}\delta_{j,m_{3}}\delta_{j,m_{4}}+m_{1}\leftrightarrow m_{2}+m_{1}\leftrightarrow m_{3}+m_{1}\leftrightarrow m_{4}\big)
+O⁡(x2).\displaystyle+O(x^{2})\ . (53)

Inserting this expansion into Eq. (50), we obtain that in the strong-field limit, the Hamiltonian (1) may be rigorously approximated by

H^\displaystyle\hat{H} ≈F∑mmb^m†b^m+V∑jb^m†b^mb^m+1†b^m+1+x​V2∑mb^m†b^m(b^m−2†b^m−1+b^m+2†b^m+1+h.c.).\displaystyle\approx F\sum_{m}m\;\hat{b}_{m}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{m}+V\sum_{j}\;\hat{b}_{m}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{m}\hat{b}_{m+1}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{m+1}+\frac{xV}{2}\sum_{m}\hat{b}_{m}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{m}\big(\hat{b}_{m-2}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{m-1}+\hat{b}_{m+2}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{m+1}+h.c.\big)\ . (54)

which is similar to Eq. (21) in [42]. The last term in Eq. (54) provides a kind of many-body hopping term (since the hopping only happens if site mm is occupied) that gives a hint of how the strong-field non-interacting ground-state with all sites till (above) a given site having unit (zero) occupancy is disturbed by the interaction VV, moving electrons from the left towards the right side of the chain. This term will increase the characteristic length of the occupancy wall, as numerically observed. A schematic representation of this many-body hopping term is given in Fig. (14).
